messages.content: You are the neutral rapporteur of a technology readiness review panel. Consolidate, attribute and preserve disagreement; do not decide and do not add technical claims of your own.

# Synthesis: assess · T05

## Claude Opus 5.5


# TRL assessment: T05 Microgravity beneficiation of native Fe-Ni

## 0. Requirement restated, and a check on the balance

T05 covers the on-site step that turns excavated NEA regolith into a metal-rich concentrate. That means comminution to liberation, low-intensity magnetic separation (possibly with electrostatic or size pre-concentration), and grain transport and containment in microgravity. It does not cover the downstream metallurgy (carbonyl, H₂ reduction or rotating smelting), which feeds from T05.

The architecture's ranges only close if they are paired. They do not close if read independently:

| Case | Feed (kt/yr) | Concentrate (kt/yr) | Tailings (kt/yr) | Ratio | Delivered product (kt/yr) | Downstream yield implied |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Low | 15 | 2 | 13 | 7.5:1 | 0.6 | 30% of concentrate |
| High | 55 | 8 | 47 | 6.9:1 | 2.5 | 31% of concentrate |
| Unpaired extremes | 15–55 | 2–8 | — | 1.9–27.5:1 | — | — |

The tailings figure of 13–47 kt/yr is consistent only with the paired cases. So the reconciled balance actually implies **about 7:1 at both ends**, not "anywhere in 4–15:1". GPT's 4:1 (25% mass yield) and Claude's 15:1 bound lie outside the balance the architecture adopted. I keep the 4–15:1 envelope as the requirement but flag that 7:1 is the design point the other numbers assume.

**Feed-grade check.** These are approximate bulk metal contents, which I hold with medium confidence. The basis is the compilation by Jarosewich (1990, *Meteoritics* 25) and standard ordinary-chondrite classification:

| Type | Fe-Ni metal (wt%) |
|---|---|
| H | ~15–19 |
| L | ~5–9 |
| LL | ~1–3 |

- **L feed (~8%), high case.** 55 kt feed contains ~4.4 kt metal. An 8 kt concentrate at 50% grade then requires ~90% recovery. That is plausible.
- **LL feed (~2%), high case.** 55 kt feed contains ~1.1 kt metal. This cannot support 2.5 kt/yr delivered at any recovery. LL feed closes only near the low case, and only with high recovery.
- **Itokawa.** The only sampled S-type is LL-like (see Evidence). The best-characterised analogue is therefore the one that breaks the high end of the balance.
- **H feed (~18%), low case.** 15 kt feed contains ~2.7 kt metal. A 2 kt concentrate at 70% grade needs only ~50% recovery. Ratio is easy, and grade is the binding constraint.
- **M-type branch.** Feed is metal-dominated. The meaningful operation is silicate rejection, and the ratio will be about 1.2–2:1. **Claude's "<3:1 breaks co-location" falsifier applies to chondritic feed only.** It must not be applied to an M-type target, where a low ratio is the expected and benign outcome.

**Ratio alone is an incomplete specification.** It must be paired with grade, recovery and liberation size. I rate against all four.

**Required throughput.** 15–55 kt/yr is 1.7–6.3 t/h continuous. At 50% plant availability it is 3.4–12.6 t/h. Duration is multi-year operation, assumed at 5–10 yr.

**Liberation.** In ordinary chondrites much of the metal occurs as grains of tens of µm up to ~1 mm. It is often intergrown with troilite or bonded in silicate. Liberation adequate for >80% recovery probably requires grinding to roughly 100–300 µm. That is my estimate from chondrite petrography, not a measured liberation curve on representative feed. No such curve exists, and that gap is the core of rq-0-51.

---

## 1. Evidence

| # | Claim | Source | Demonstrated scale / environment | Ratio to required | Confident |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| E1 | The sampled S-type NEA regolith is LL-chondrite material: thermally metamorphosed, metal-poor, with particles ~tens–hundreds µm | Nakamura et al. 2011, *Science* 333 (Hayabusa/Itokawa); Tsuchiyama et al. 2011, *Science* 333 (3-D structure) | µg–mg of returned grains; characterisation only, no separation | n/a (feed definition, not process) | Yes |
| E2 | Bulk metal contents of H/L/LL chondrites | Jarosewich 1990, *Meteoritics* 25, compilation of meteorite analyses | Laboratory analyses | n/a (feed definition) | Yes for the source; medium for my exact percentages |
| E3 | Fe-Ni metal can be separated from chondrite silicate with a hand magnet or lab magnetic separator after crushing | Routine meteoritics laboratory practice for siderophile and metal-phase analysis | Grams, batch, 1 g, air | ~10⁹–10¹⁰ (kt/yr ÷ g batch) | Yes as practice. **No specific paper cited, and none reports grade or recovery against a prediction** |
| E4 | Magnetic beneficiation of lunar soils (separating glass, agglutinates and minerals, including npFe-bearing fractions) | Oder & Taylor 1990, "Magnetic beneficiation of highland and hi-Ti mare soils", *Space 90* (ASCE) proceedings | Grams–kg of Apollo soil, 1 g | ~10⁷–10⁹ | **Not fully.** I believe this paper exists with that scope but cannot verify the details |
| E5 | Electrostatic beneficiation of lunar simulant, possibly including reduced-gravity flights | NASA KSC electrostatics laboratory work, 2000s–2010s | Bench, kg/h | ~10³–10⁴ | **No.** I know of the KSC programme but cannot cite a specific paper or confirm the parabolic-flight element |
| E6 | Granular flow behaves qualitatively differently in microgravity; convection is suppressed or altered | Murdoch et al. 2013, *Phys. Rev. Lett.* 110, 018307 (parabolic flight) | ~20 s µg, cm-scale cell | n/a (physics, not separator) | Yes |
| E7 | For sub-mm grains on asteroids, cohesion and electrostatics dominate gravity | Scheeres et al. 2010, *Icarus* 210 | Analysis | n/a (sets design regime) | Yes |
| E8 | Regolith can be acquired and contained in microgravity at gram scale | Hayabusa2 (Ryugu, ~5.4 g returned 2020); OSIRIS-REx TAGSAM (Bennu, ~122 g returned 2023) | g, single event, no separation | ~10⁸ by mass per year | Yes |
| E9 | Industrial dry low-intensity magnetic separation of ferromagnetic material at ≥ t/h | Terrestrial iron-ore and scrap practice (drum and belt LIMS) | 10–1000 t/h, 1 g, air | Throughput <1× (exceeds requirement); environment unrepresentative | Yes as practice, no specific citation |

**What is absent:**
- No test of continuous magnetic separation of native metal in microgravity.
- No grade/recovery/throughput curve on representative chondritic feed with realistic metal attachment.
- No ordinary-chondrite simulant with realistic metal grain size and attachment. Existing asteroid simulants are CI/CM-based, e.g. Britt et al. 2019, *Meteoritics & Planetary Science*, which I am fairly but not fully confident of. These contain essentially no native metal.
- No DEM model of a magnetic separator in microgravity validated against test data.
- No vacuum abrasion or life test of a separator on chondritic feed.

Concept literature does not count toward TRL ≥3: Lewis, *Mining the Sky* (1996); Kargel 1994 (*JGR*, metal asteroids); commercial asteroid-mining design studies; and the panel's own chains.

---

## 2. Current TRL: 2–3

- **TRL 2, met (lower bound).** The application is documented in panel material and older concept literature: magnetic concentration of native Fe-Ni at the NEA with a stated ratio and feed envelope. The underlying separation physics also has peer-reviewed grounding (E3/E4 for separation, E6/E7 for the regime).
- **TRL 3, partially met (upper bound).** The critical separation function (native metal being strongly ferromagnetic and separable with LIMS) is experimentally proven in 1 g at gram scale. That is the reason for the upper bound of 3.
- **Why the range does not collapse to 3.** The exit criterion is "documented analytical or experimental results validating predictions of key parameters". No document I can cite predicts grade and recovery as a function of liberation size for chondritic feed and then measures them. The second critical function, controlled grain transport and feed presentation in microgravity, has only physics-level evidence (E6). There is no separator-level evidence at all.

**Unmet exit criterion for TRL 3:** documented experimental results validating predicted grade, recovery and liberation for representative feed (LL/L/H, realistic metal attachment) at a stated throughput.

**Unmet exit criterion for TRL 4:** a breadboard separator, comminution plus feed plus magnetic stage, tested in the laboratory with performance agreeing with predictions, together with a documented definition of the relevant environment. That definition covers microgravity feed dynamics, vacuum, triboelectric charging, thermal range and abrasion.

**Rated by downstream route.** The TRL is the same (2–3) for all routes. The required concentrate specification differs, so difficulty differs. The grade figures below are my assumptions and need confirmation from the metallurgy assessments.

| Route | Concentrate need (assumed) | Effect on T05 |
|---|---|---|
| Claude, no-melt (magnetic → carbonyl / H₂) | Moderate–high grade (~50–80% metal); exposed, unoxidised metal surfaces; troilite and space-weathered rims matter (sulfur interaction with carbonylation is chemistry I am unsure of) | Hardest on liberation and surface condition |
| Gemini, rotating 0.05–0.15 g smelting | Tolerates lower grade (~30–50%); silicate becomes slag | Easiest on T05; shifts burden to the furnace (separate technology) |
| GPT, narrow native-metal product | Highest grade (≥80–90%) if the concentrate is near-product | Hardest on grade; may need multi-stage cleaning |
| M-type branch | Silicate rejection at ~1.2–2:1; metal comminution difficult (ductile) | Different machine; untested; no sampled M-type until Psyche (arrival ~2029) |

---

## 3. Target and difficulty

**Target.** T05 is project-ending for 0B, because co-location depends on it and central processing has been abandoned (see §5). Under D-02 it therefore needs **TRL 6 at KDP-0B**: a subsystem prototype in a relevant environment, with no waivers.

**Internal 0A milestone.** TRL 4 at the 0A mid-term review and TRL 5 before pathfinder design freeze.

**Dates.** No KDP dates are given. I assume a 0A mid-term around 2029–2030 and KDP-0B around 2033–2036. Treat these as assumptions.

**Practical constraint on reaching TRL 6.** It almost certainly needs the 0A pathfinder at an NEA, or a long-duration free-flyer in vacuum with validated simulant. Parabolic flight (~20 s) and drop towers (~5–9 s) cannot demonstrate continuous separation. If the pathfinder slips, T05 slips with it.

**AD²: 6** (several competing approaches; path not clear; ≈60%). The reasons:
- The magnetic step is low risk because native metal is about the easiest magnetic separation there is. On its own it would rate AD² 3–4.
- The difficulty is the microgravity system. Feed presentation could be mechanical, centrifugal, vibratory or rotating-drum. A pre-concentration stage, or none, is also open. Comminution of a mix of ductile metal and brittle silicate is unsolved for this setting. Containment of fines must meet a debris ceiling of ≤1 t/yr escaped against 15–55 kt/yr throughput, i.e. losses ≤ ~2–7×10⁻⁵ of feed. Magnetic flocculation will entrain silicate.
- These approaches compete, and none has been tested.
- I would move this to **AD² 7** for an LL-only target or for the M-type branch, and to **AD² 5** if paired with the smelting route.

---

## 4. Path

| Step | Method | Scale | Cost (USD) | Duration (yr) | Reaches |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1. Feed characterisation: metal grain-size and attachment statistics from Itokawa grains (via JAXA curation announcement of opportunity) and from minimally weathered H/L/LL falls; X-ray CT, SEM/EBSD; liberation-size curves | Literature + experiment | mg–kg | 0.3–1.0 M | 1–2 | Enables TRL 3 |
| P2. Representative feed: (a) crushed real ordinary chondrites, weathering grade W0–W1, 10–200 kg (unclassified ordinary chondrites are commercially available at modest cost per gram; weathered finds have oxidised metal and must be screened); (b) engineered simulant with metal bonded in silicate and clay matrices (Gemini's falsifier case) | Experiment | 10–500 kg | 0.5–2 M | 1–2 | Supports TRL 3 |
| P3. 1 g lab breadboard: comminution plus dry LIMS; grade/recovery/ratio against throughput and grind size; predictions documented beforehand | Experiment | 10–100 kg/h | 1–4 M | 1–2 | **TRL 3 → 4** (with environment definition) |
| P4. DEM of separator grain transport with cohesion, magnetic dipole and triboelectric forces; calibrate on P3 and P5 | Simulation | Separator-scale | 0.5–2 M | 1–3 | Supports TRL 4–5 (bounds throughput; not evidence alone) |
| P5. Short-duration reduced-gravity tests of feed presentation and magnetic capture (parabolic flight; ZARM drop tower with evacuated capsule) | Experiment | g–kg, 5–20 s | 1–3 M | 1–2 | Component-level relevant environment; partial TRL 5 |
| P6. Thermal-vacuum and abrasion life test of breadboard on chondritic feed, ≥2,000 h | Experiment | 10–100 kg/h | 2–6 M | 1–2 | Supports TRL 5 (life, wear, charging) |
| P7. Long-duration microgravity, vacuum separation experiment (ISS external platform or free-flyer); continuous operation for months; documented scaling requirements | Experiment | 0.1–1 kg/h | 15–60 M | 3–5 | **TRL 5** |
| P8. 0A pathfinder demonstrator at target NEA: subsystem prototype on real regolith for months, measuring ratio, grade, recovery and fines escape | Experiment (flight) | 1–10 kg/h (170–6,300× below required) | 50–200 M (T05 share of pathfinder) | 4–7 incl. development | **TRL 6** (arguably 7 if flight-representative; see §6) |

The result feeds rq-0-61 (the mass-balance and delivered-cost model) and closes rq-0-10 (on-robot versus at-plant separation).

---

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Risk class: project-ending (for 0B).**
- Co-location depends on concentrating at the site.
- Central SEL4/5 ore processing is abandoned, so there is no architectural home for unconcentrated ore.
- A ratio below ~3:1 on chondritic feed, or a grade too low for the selected downstream route, fails the economics gate.
- It is **architecture-change** rather than project-ending if an H-chondrite or M-type target is available. On those targets a low ratio is acceptable, or the requirement inverts.

**Fallback.** In order of preference:
1. Retarget to metal-richer feed (H or M-type), using the D-02 target gate (sampled grade).
2. Pair with the smelting route, which tolerates lower grade.
3. Revert to D-02's pre-committed "0A only, Earth supply".

---

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **Upper bound of 3 vs. firm 3.** One could argue that magnetic separation of native Fe-Ni is so well understood (E3, E9) that the critical function is proven and TRL is 3, possibly 4, for the separation step. My counter is that TRL attaches to the function at the required environment. Microgravity feed presentation is a critical function, and nothing at separator level exists for it. Splitting T05 into a "separation" element and a "microgravity handling" element would resolve this. I recommend that split.
2. **The ratio metric itself.** Claude's 3:1 falsifier and GPT's 4:1 are feed-dependent. On M-type feed they are meaningless. On LL feed even 15:1 may not close the balance. I would replace the requirement with grade ≥ X at recovery ≥ Y on the sampled target's feed. The architecture currently specifies a ratio.
3. **The architecture's own balance.** The adopted figures pin ~7:1. The 4–15:1 envelope partly reflects unreconciled model positions. The disagreement is preserved here, not averaged: GPT at 4:1, Gemini at 5–8:1, Claude at 5–15:1.
4. **Is a 170–6,300× scaled-down pathfinder sufficient for TRL 6?** I accept it, provided TRL 5 documented scaling requirements, as NPR 7123.1 and ECSS practice allow. A strict reviewer could hold that grain-transport physics does not scale simply with cohesion-dominated fines. On that view TRL 6 would need ≥ ~100 kg/h, which would raise pathfinder mass and power considerably.
5. **Simulant validity.** Using crushed real meteorites is defensible for mineralogy. However, terrestrial weathering and the absence of space-weathering rims (npFe on silicates, which raises silicate magnetic susceptibility and lowers grade) mean ground results may be optimistic. Only real NEA regolith resolves this, which again puts T05's TRL 6 on the pathfinder's critical path.

## Gemini 3.1 Pro


### 1. Evidence
Terrestrial dry magnetic separation is a mature (TRL 9) technology for mining, but microgravity beneficiation of asteroid regolith lacks large-scale physical validation. Basic principles of magnetic separation for lunar and asteroid simulants have been demonstrated in 1g laboratory environments, and limited electrostatic/magnetic particle behavior has been observed in drop towers and parabolic flights (e.g., early work by Oder on lunar soils, and various NASA NIAC studies on asteroid ISRU). However, I am unsure of any specific, peer-reviewed parabolic flight campaign that successfully demonstrated continuous magnetic beneficiation of Fe-Ni from a silicate matrix at a measurable concentration ratio in microgravity. 

The demonstrated scale in 1g lab tests is typically on the order of grams to kilograms per hour. The required scale is 15–55 kt/yr feed (approx. 1.7–6.2 tonnes per hour). The scale ratio is therefore roughly 1,000:1 to 10,000:1.

### 2. Current TRL
**TRL 3–4.** 
Analytical and experimental critical function proof-of-concept exists in 1g (TRL 3). Some breadboard validation in laboratory environments (vacuum, 1g) may push this to TRL 4. 
*Unmet exit criterion for TRL 5:* Documented test performance of a component/breadboard in a relevant environment (microgravity/vacuum) agreeing with predictions, and documented definition of scaling requirements.

### 3. Target and Difficulty
**Target TRL:** 6 at KDP-0B (project-ending for Phase 0B if the concentration ratio falls below 3:1).
**AD²:** 5. New development; similar development has not been done in microgravity, but the path is clear (terrestrial magnetic separation physics is well understood, though particle flow and clearing without gravity require new engineering).

### 4. Path
1. **Simulant development & 1g baselining:** Create LL/L/H and M-type simulants with realistic sub-mm liberation characteristics. Run through 1g dry magnetic separators to establish baseline grade/recovery. (Scale: 10–100 kg/hr; Cost: $0.5M–$1M; Duration: 1 yr; Reaches TRL 4).
2. **Microgravity parabolic flight campaign:** Test breadboard magnetic/electrostatic separators in parabolic flights to validate particle transport, separation efficiency, and clearing mechanisms without gravity. (Scale: 1–10 kg/hr; Cost: $1M–$3M; Duration: 1–2 yrs; Reaches TRL 5).
3. **Pathfinder demonstrator (0A):** In-space demonstration on the 0A pathfinder vehicle at a target NEA to validate continuous operation, concentration ratio (4-15:1), and throughput in true environment. (Scale: 100–500 kg/hr; Cost: $50M–$150M; Duration: 2–3 yrs; Reaches TRL 6).

### 5. Risk and Fallback
**Risk:** Project-ending. If the concentration ratio falls below 3:1, the co-located processing architecture fails, mass economics break, and the delivered-cost model for Phase 0B cannot close.
**Fallback:** 0A only, Earth supply.

### 6. Where others might disagree
The assumption that dry magnetic separation can be scaled to 6 t/h in microgravity without massive dust mitigation and jamming issues. Terrestrial systems rely heavily on gravity to clear non-magnetic tailings from the drum/belt; replacing this with centrifugal or pneumatic forces in a vacuum may drastically increase power and complexity, potentially lowering the current realistic TRL to 2 for the *microgravity continuous flow* aspect.

## GPT-6.1 Sol


## T05 — Microgravity beneficiation of native Fe–Ni

**Assessment: TRL 2–3; AD² 6 to reach TRL 6.** Magnetic separation has a strong terrestrial physical basis, but I cannot substantiate an integrated demonstration of liberation, selective recovery, continuous solids transport and tailings containment for representative asteroid feed in microgravity.

The **lower bound, TRL 2, is supported for the integrated application**. The upper bound, TRL 3, is defensible for magnetic discrimination as a critical function—not for the complete beneficiation train. No panel agreement or mass-flow model raises that rating.

This is **project-ending for the native-metal 0B option if no qualifying target/process combination is demonstrated**. It is not project-ending for 0A, which can finish as a research and reconnaissance programme.

---

## 1. Required performance and reconciled balance

### Definitions and assumptions

I interpret **4–15:1 concentration as feed mass divided by concentrate mass**, not as grade enrichment:

\[
R=F/C,\qquad Cg_c=Fg_f r_b,\qquad D=Cg_c\eta_m\eta_d
\]

where:

- \(F,C,D\): annual feed, concentrate and delivered metal;
- \(g_f,g_c\): recoverable native Fe–Ni feed grade and concentrate grade;
- \(r_b\): beneficiation recovery;
- \(\eta_m,\eta_d\): subsequent metallurgical and delivery yields.

“Recoverable native metal” must exclude iron bound in silicates, sulfides or oxides unless a separately qualified conversion process is included.

### One internally closed reference balance

These are **requirements for testing, not demonstrated performance**.

| Stream or parameter | Reference value |
|---|---:|
| Feed | 30 kt/yr |
| Native Fe–Ni feed grade | 10 wt% |
| Beneficiation recovery | 66.7% |
| Concentrate | 4 kt/yr |
| Concentrate native-metal grade | 50 wt% |
| Feed/concentrate ratio | 7.5:1 |
| Beneficiation tailings | 26 kt/yr |
| Metal entering subsequent processing | 2 kt/yr |
| Combined subsequent processing/delivery yield | 75% |
| Delivered Fe–Ni | 1.5 kt/yr |
| Subsequent processing residue/loss allowance | 2.5 kt/yr |

The last allowance must be divided experimentally into contained residue, rejected impurities, retained inventory and actual loss. It is **not permission to discharge material**.

The requested envelopes—**15–55 kt/yr feed, 2–8 kt/yr concentrate and 4–15:1 mass concentration**—are compatible only as selected combinations, not as independent ranges. The reference balance falls within all three.

For sizing, assuming **4,000–6,000 operating hours/year**, the separator train needs approximately **2.5–13.8 t/h**. I assume a **five-year service life**, or **20,000–30,000 operating hours**; the supplied architecture does not establish a plant lifetime, so this remains a requirement to ratify.

### Feed branches must remain separate

- **LL/L/H ordinary-chondrite envelope:** test actual differences in native-metal abundance, grain size, intergrowth and weathering. Do not substitute total iron abundance for recoverable metal.
- **Low-metal LL-like feed:** may fail the delivered-product requirement despite achieving a high feed/concentrate ratio. At 2 wt% native metal, 30 kt/yr contains only 0.6 kt/yr before any losses.
- **M-type branch:** neither spectral classification nor radar reflectivity establishes sampled native-metal grade or liberation. A genuinely metal-rich target may need sorting rather than strong mass concentration.
- **Mass-conservation constraint:** \(R g_f r_b\leq1\). At 80 wt% native metal and near-total recovery, the maximum feed/concentrate ratio is only about 1.25:1. Requiring 4–15:1 on that branch would mean rejecting useful metal.

“Sub-mm liberation” must mean **measured liberation of metal grains**, not merely crushing everything below 1 mm.

---

## 2. Evidence supporting the current rating

| Evidence | Demonstrated scale and environment | Required ÷ demonstrated | What it supports—and does not |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Rosenblum and Brownfield, _Magnetic Susceptibilities of Minerals_, USGS Open-File Report 99-529, 1999** | Laboratory mineral susceptibility/separation measurements; terrestrial gravity. I do not have a verified continuous throughput or test charge mass from this report. | **n/a:** no comparable production throughput established. | Supports magnetic discrimination as an experimentally grounded principle. Does not establish asteroid native-metal grade/recovery, liberation or microgravity operation. |
| **NASA Surveyor programme, particularly Surveyor VII, 1968** | Magnetic material collection from lunar soil using magnet-equipped apparatus; lunar vacuum and approximately 0.16 g. | **n/a:** collection experiment, not a quantified beneficiation stream. | Physical evidence that magnetic interactions can collect extraterrestrial granular material. Magnetic attraction does not prove selective recovery of native Fe–Ni rather than other magnetic phases. |
| **Nakamura et al., “Itokawa Dust Particles: A Direct Link Between S-Type Asteroids and Ordinary Chondrites,” _Science_, 2011; Hayabusa sample return, 2010** | Microscopic returned asteroid particles; laboratory mineralogical characterization. No beneficiation train. | **n/a:** feed characterization, not process throughput. | Supports ordinary-chondrite-like target material and the need to characterize real particles. Does not demonstrate industrial liberation or recovery. |
| **Jarosewich, “Chemical Analyses of Meteorites: A Compilation of Stony and Iron Meteorite Analyses,” _Meteoritics_, 1990** | Laboratory chemical analyses of meteorite specimens. No operational separator demonstration. | **n/a.** | Supports composition variability and the need for separate feed branches. Bulk chemistry alone does not determine native-metal liberation. |

**Evidence limitation:** I am not confident enough in a specific published microgravity native-Fe–Ni beneficiation test to cite one. Consequently, there is **no substantiated demonstrated/required production-throughput ratio**. It would be misleading to infer one from mineral-analysis specimens or magnetic collection experiments.

Terrestrial industrial magnetic separation is mature, but its gravity-assisted feeding, stratification, discharge and reject handling cannot simply be assigned the same TRL in microgravity.

---

## 3. Current TRL and separate route assessments

| Technology boundary | Current TRL | Supported exit criterion / missing next criterion |
|---|---:|---|
| **Integrated liberation → magnetic/size separation → contained concentrate and tailings** | **2–3** | TRL 2: documented application and physically credible benefit. TRL 3 upper bound applies to magnetic discrimination only. Integrated TRL 3 still needs test-validated predictions of grade, recovery, throughput and containment. TRL 4 needs a representative-feed breadboard with measured performance agreeing with predictions and a defined relevant environment. |
| **Claude: beneficiation → carbonyl refining, without bulk melting** | **2–3** | Terrestrial carbonyl chemistry is established, but an asteroid-feed, closed-reagent, autonomous vacuum process is not substantiated here. No integrated laboratory validation is established. |
| **Claude: beneficiation → H₂ reduction** | **2** for this application | Reduction applies to reducible compounds, not to already-native metal. The feed phases, temperature, hydrogen recycling and water/by-product handling must first be specified. Oxide-derived metal must remain a separate qualification branch. |
| **Gemini: rotating 0.05–0.15 g smelting furnace** | **2–3** | Melting and centrifugal force are established individually. I have no verified test of the proposed integrated furnace using representative concentrate, with vacuum heat balance, phase separation, tapping and containment. |
| **GPT: narrow native-metal production, rotating modules experimentally gated** | **2–3** | Narrowing the feed chemistry lowers development scope, not the evidence threshold. A rotating separator or transport module still requires physical validation. Adding melting brings back the furnace qualification burden. |

For the carbonyl route, established **Mond-process chemistry** is heritage, not proof of the proposed plant. Feed impurities, reagent losses, deposition control and gas containment could dominate. No-melt is not synonymous with low-complexity.

### Target, timing and difficulty

- **Internal 0A milestone:** TRL **4**, followed by **5** after relevant-environment breadboard testing.
- **KDP-0B:** TRL **6**, without waiver, for beneficiation and whichever downstream production route is selected.
- **Needed by:** the KDP-0B authorization decision. No calendar date is supplied.
- **Indicative development time:** **6–10 years from funded start**, conditional on flight access and a qualifying target.
- **AD²:** **6** for T05: several plausible transport/separation approaches exist, but their performance under asteroid conditions is unresolved.
- **Route-specific AD²:** carbonyl **6–7**; H₂ conversion **6–7** if retained; rotating smelting **7**; narrow native-metal separation **6**. These use the project’s working anchors, not calibrated probabilities.

The furnace route is harder because it adds molten-material containment, heat transfer, phase separation and controlled product discharge. No route should inherit another route’s TRL.

---

## 4. Development path

Costs below are **rough-order-of-magnitude planning allowances in USD**, not quotations. Tests overlap; their costs and durations should not be mechanically summed.

| Step | Scale and discriminating measurements | Cost | Duration | TRL reached |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **Feed and evidence audit** | Review verified separation literature; characterize meteorites and construct separate LL/L/H feed envelopes. Establish native-metal assay, liberation and mineral-specific magnetic response. | $0.3–1.2M | 0.5–1 yr | 2–3 |
| **Laboratory integrated breadboard** | 10–100 kg/h; tens to hundreds of kilograms per feed class. Test bonded/intergrown metal, not only loose iron mixed with sand. Measure grade, recovery, specific energy, fines, wear and closed mass balance. | $2–7M | 1–2 yr | 4 |
| **Test-calibrated transport model** | DEM/magnetic-force/contact model calibrated against the breadboard, including cohesion, charging and discharge. Extrapolate to 2.5–13.8 t/h with uncertainty bounds. | $0.5–2M | 1–2 yr, parallel | Supports 4; no independent TRL increment |
| **Vacuum and reduced-gravity breadboard** | Approximately 1–10 kg batches in drop-tower/parabolic tests, plus longer vacuum/thermal campaigns. Test start/stop, wall adhesion, segregation, release and containment. | $3–10M | 1–2 yr | 5 only with documented scaling requirements |
| **Endurance and scaled-module campaign** | Approximately 0.1–1 t/h ground modules; 2,000–5,000 h endurance, abrasive feed and representative vacuum/thermal conditions. Quantify replacement intervals and justified extrapolation to full life. | $8–25M | 2–3 yr | 5 |
| **0A flight pathfinder** | Complete closed train at approximately 10–100 kg/h; cumulative 10–100 t processed and months of operation, subject to mission capability. Representative asteroid feed is strongly preferred. | $80–250M allocated programme allowance | 3–6 yr | 6, conditional on defensible scaling |
| **Selected downstream-route qualification** | Separately test carbonyl, H₂ conversion if applicable, or rotating furnace with the qualified concentrate. Include reagent/heat balances, product assay and residue containment. | $10–50M | 2–4 yr | 4–5; flight integration needed for 6 |

The flight pathfinder would remain **25–1,380 times below required instantaneous throughput**, depending on the compared endpoints. A TRL 6 claim therefore needs a credible modular scale-up argument—not merely successful operation of a small separator.

### Acceptance measurements

Before testing, set quantitative acceptance criteria for:

1. **Delivered metal**, not concentration ratio alone.
2. Native-metal grade and recovery for each qualified feed class.
3. Liberation energy and achievable throughput.
4. Total escaped mass across excavation, transfer, separation and tailings storage.
5. Power, consumables, wear and autonomous fault recovery.
6. Traceable mass balance with uncertainty smaller than the recovery differences being evaluated.

The proposed **≤1 t/yr site-wide escape ceiling** permits only about **21–77 ppm of the 13–47 kt/yr beneficiation tailings stream** if the entire allowance were assigned to tailings. In practice, beneficiation receives less than the whole site allowance. A separator that concentrates well but sheds fines fails the architectural requirement.

---

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Primary risk class: project-ending for native-metal 0B.**

Failure can mean:

- insufficient sampled native-metal grade;
- unacceptable liberation energy;
- recovery collapse when throughput increases;
- inability to move and discharge solids reliably in microgravity;
- unacceptable dust escape;
- inability to operate autonomously for the required life.

**Fallback hierarchy:**

1. Select a better-characterized target and re-size production against signed demand.
2. Use experimentally validated rotating confinement or enclosed forced transport—an **architecture change**, not a presumed solution.
3. Restrict production to coarse, naturally liberated native metal at a lower rate.
4. If no route meets the target, demand, economics and licence gates, execute **“0A only, Earth supply.”**

A ratio below 3:1 is **not a universal physical falsifier**. It is potentially fatal to a low-grade-feed logistics model, but a genuinely metal-rich target can deliver useful metal at a much lower feed/concentrate ratio. Grade, recovery and downstream yield must decide the gate.

---

## 6. Where others might disagree

- **TRL 3 versus TRL 2:** assessors may credit magnetic discrimination as sufficient critical-function proof. I retain TRL 2 for the integrated train because transport, liberation and containment remain unvalidated.
- **Artificial gravity as a shortcut:** rotating confinement could make separation more terrestrial-like. It does not remove vacuum, charging, transfer, wear or tailings-disposal requirements.
- **How much scale-up supports TRL 6:** a small flight unit may qualify a modular design if scaling is demonstrated. It cannot qualify an arbitrarily larger monolithic plant.
- **Feed representativeness:** loose metal-in-sand simulants can substantially overstate liberation and recovery.
- **Route ranking:** carbonyl may avoid a furnace but introduce demanding reagent and gas-management systems. The evidence does not yet establish a clear winner.
- **The old rq-0-10 assumptions:** central bulk-ore transport and generic asteroid-type “extractable” percentages are superseded or unverified inputs, not evidence for this assessment.

# Consolidated rating: T05, microgravity beneficiation of native Fe-Ni

**Rapporteur's note.** This consolidates three assessments: Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro and GPT-6.1 Sol. Every claim below is attributed to the model that made it. Where the models diverge, the divergence is kept, and the test, source or panel ruling that would settle it is named. No new technical claims are added.

---

## 1. Summary of ratings

| | Claude Opus 5.5 | Gemini 3.1 Pro | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Current TRL** | 2–3 | **3–4** | 2–3 |
| **Basis for upper bound** | TRL 3 only for the magnetic separation function in 1 g. No separator-level evidence for microgravity feed presentation. | 1 g proof of concept gives 3. "Some breadboard validation… (vacuum, 1g) may push this to TRL 4." No breadboard is cited. | TRL 3 only for magnetic discrimination. The integrated train is at 2. |
| **AD² to target** | 6. Would be 7 for an LL-only or M-type target, 5 if paired with smelting. | 5 ("path is clear") | 6. Route-specific: carbonyl 6–7, H₂ 6–7, rotating smelting 7, narrow native-metal 6. |
| **Target** | TRL 6 at KDP-0B, no waiver. Internal milestones: TRL 4 at 0A mid-term, TRL 5 before pathfinder design freeze. | TRL 6 at KDP-0B | TRL 6 at KDP-0B, no waiver. Internal milestones: TRL 4 then 5 in 0A. |
| **Assumed dates** | 0A mid-term ~2029–2030; KDP-0B ~2033–2036 (stated as assumptions) | None given | None ("calendar date unspecified") |
| **Risk class** | Project-ending for 0B. Becomes architecture-change if an H-chondrite or M-type target is available. | Project-ending if the ratio falls below 3:1 | Project-ending for the native-metal 0B option. Explicitly not project-ending for 0A. |
| **Years to target** | 6–12 | **3–5** | 6–10 |
| **Fallback** | (1) Retarget to H or M-type; (2) pair with smelting; (3) "0A only, Earth supply" | "0A only, Earth supply" | (1) Retarget or resize; (2) validated rotating or forced transport (architecture change); (3) coarse native metal at lower rate; (4) "0A only, Earth supply" |
| **Confidence** | Medium | Medium | Medium |
| **Related RQs** | rq-0-51, rq-0-10, rq-0-61 | rq-0-51, rq-0-10 | rq-0-51, rq-0-10 |

**Consolidated envelope (not a decision):**
- Current TRL: 2–4. Two models give 2–3; one gives 3–4.
- AD²: 5–6.
- Target: TRL 6 at KDP-0B (unanimous).
- Risk: project-ending for 0B (unanimous), with differing qualifiers.
- Years to target: 3–12. Two models give 6–10 or 6–12; one gives 3–5.

---

## 2. Where the models agree

1. **Target.** All three require TRL 6 at KDP-0B.
2. **Risk class.** All three say failure is project-ending for 0B, and all three end the fallback chain at "0A only, Earth supply".
3. **Terrestrial heritage.** All three say terrestrial dry magnetic separation is mature but does not carry its TRL into microgravity. Claude and GPT tie this to gravity-assisted feeding and discharge. Gemini ties it to tailings clearing.
4. **No microgravity test exists.** None of the three cites a demonstration of continuous magnetic beneficiation of native Fe-Ni in microgravity. Gemini and GPT both state explicitly that they cannot cite one.
5. **The hard part is grain handling.** All three place the critical difficulty in microgravity grain transport, feed presentation, discharge and containment, not in magnetic discrimination itself. Gemini's §6 concedes the "microgravity continuous flow aspect" could be TRL 2.
6. **Simulants.** All three call for representative feed or simulants covering LL, L and H material. Claude and GPT both warn that loose metal-in-sand or CI/CM simulants would overstate performance.
7. **Pathfinder.** All three make the 0A pathfinder at an NEA the step that reaches TRL 6.
8. **Breadboard scale.** All three use 10–100 kg/h for the 1 g lab breadboard.
9. **Throughput.** Claude and Gemini both give about 1.7–6.3 t/h continuous for 15–55 kt/yr. GPT gives 2.5–13.8 t/h, and Claude gives 3.4–12.6 t/h, once availability is accounted for. The two figures differ only by the availability assumption.
10. **Mass balance (Claude and GPT only).**
    - The 15–55 / 2–8 kt/yr / 4–15:1 ranges close only as paired combinations.
    - Both land near 7:1: Claude derives ~7:1 from the architecture's paired cases; GPT's reference balance gives 7.5:1.
    - Ratio alone is an insufficient specification. Grade, recovery and liberation must be specified with it.
    - LL-like feed (~2 wt% metal) may fail to deliver enough product even at a high ratio.
    - On M-type feed, the requirement inverts (Claude gives ~1.2–2:1; GPT gives ≤~1.25:1 at 80 wt%).
    - The 3:1 falsifier is not universal.
11. **Debris ceiling (Claude and GPT only).** Both convert the ≤1 t/yr escape ceiling into a loss fraction: Claude gives ~2–7×10⁻⁵ of feed; GPT gives 21–77 ppm of the tailings stream. The denominators differ but the figures are consistent.

---

## 3. Where the models diverge, and why

### D1. Current TRL: 2–3 (Claude, GPT) versus 3–4 (Gemini)

- **Gemini's basis:** 1 g proof of concept, plus a possible vacuum/1 g breadboard. Its single evidence item ("Oder et al. 1990s", "General NASA ISRU studies") is marked `confident: false`. No breadboard report is cited. Gemini's own §6 also suggests TRL 2 for the continuous-flow aspect, which sits in tension with its 3–4.
- **Claude and GPT's basis:**
  - The TRL 3 exit criterion requires documented predictions of grade and recovery that have then been validated on representative feed. Neither can cite such a document.
  - Microgravity feed presentation is a critical function with only physics-level evidence (Claude citing Murdoch 2013).
- **What would settle it:**
  - A citable report of a breadboard separator run on representative chondritic feed with realistic metal attachment, in vacuum, that measures grade and recovery against stated predictions.
  - If such a report exists, Gemini's upper bound of 4 has support. If not, the evidence before the panel supports at most 3.
  - A panel ruling on Claude's proposal to split T05 into a "magnetic separation" element and a "microgravity handling" element would also resolve much of this. GPT's boundary table makes a similar separation.

### D2. AD²: 5 (Gemini) versus 6 (Claude, GPT)

- **Gemini:** the path is clear because the magnetic physics is understood.
- **Claude and GPT:** several feed-presentation, comminution and containment approaches compete, and none has been tested. Claude's list includes mechanical, centrifugal, vibratory and rotating-drum feed, plus an optional pre-concentration stage.
- **What would settle it:** a down-select among feed-presentation approaches, backed by the 1 g breadboard and reduced-gravity results (path steps C3 and C5 below).

### D3. Years to target: 3–5 (Gemini) versus 6–10 or 6–12 (GPT, Claude)

The gap comes from path content, not from different evidence.

**Whether parabolic flight reaches TRL 5:**
- Gemini credits it with TRL 5.
- Claude says 5–20 s campaigns "cannot demonstrate continuous separation". Claude adds a long-duration ISS or free-flyer experiment (P7: $15–60M, 3–5 yr) and a vacuum life test of ≥2,000 h.
- GPT credits reduced-gravity tests with TRL 5 "only with documented scaling requirements". GPT adds a 2,000–5,000 h scaled-module endurance campaign.

**Pathfinder duration:**
- Gemini: 2–3 yr.
- Claude: 4–7 yr, including development.
- GPT: 3–6 yr.

**What would settle it:**
- A panel ruling on whether short-duration reduced-gravity tests with documented scaling requirements satisfy TRL 5 for a continuous-flow function.
- Evidence on whether separator flow reaches steady state within a 5–20 s window would inform that ruling.

### D4. Pathfinder throughput needed to support a TRL 6 claim

| | Pathfinder scale | Cost | Comment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Gemini | 100–500 kg/h | $50–150M | — |
| GPT | 10–100 kg/h, 10–100 t cumulative | $80–250M | Requires a credible modular scale-up argument |
| Claude | 1–10 kg/h | $50–200M (T05 share) | Accepts it if TRL 5 documented the scaling requirements. Notes a strict reviewer might demand ≥~100 kg/h because cohesion-dominated fines may not scale simply. |

- **What would settle it:** a DEM model of the separator, calibrated against breadboards at two or more scales, showing whether performance extrapolates. Both Claude and GPT propose this step. A panel scale-up criterion is also needed.

### D5. Risk qualifier and the 3:1 falsifier

- **Gemini** applies "<3:1 breaks co-location" unconditionally.
- **Claude** limits it to chondritic feed and reclassifies the risk as architecture-change for H or M-type targets.
- **GPT** says a ratio below 3:1 "is not a universal physical falsifier", and limits project-ending to the native-metal 0B option.
- **What would settle it:** an architecture decision on whether the requirement is stated as a ratio or as grade ≥ X at recovery ≥ Y on sampled feed. Claude and GPT both recommend the latter. Sampled grade of the selected target, through the D-02 target gate, then determines which branch applies.

### D6. Effect of the downstream route on T05 difficulty

- **Claude** rates T05 TRL the same across routes. It calls rotating smelting the "easiest on T05" because the furnace tolerates ~30–50% grade, and gives AD² 5 for that pairing. Claude states that its concentrate-grade figures are assumptions needing confirmation from the metallurgy assessments.
- **GPT** rates rotating smelting at AD² 7, the hardest route, because it adds molten containment, heat transfer, phase separation and tapping.
- **Why they differ:** the two models draw the boundary differently. Claude rates T05 alone and treats the furnace as a separate technology; GPT rates the combined route.
- **What would settle it:**
  - A panel ruling on the T05 boundary.
  - Concentrate specifications from the downstream metallurgy assessments.

### D7. H₂ reduction route

- **Claude** lists "magnetic → carbonyl / H₂" as one no-melt route without further comment.
- **GPT** argues that H₂ reduction applies to reducible compounds, not to already-native metal. It rates that route at TRL 2 until the feed phases are specified.
- **What would settle it:** a phase specification of the concentrate entering the H₂ step, from the downstream assessment.

### D8. Service-life assumption

| | Assumed life |
|---|---|
| Claude | 5–10 yr continuous |
| Gemini | "1.5–5 yr cycles" |
| GPT | 5 yr; 20,000–30,000 operating hours |

All three treat this as an assumption, not an architecture input. The panel must ratify a plant lifetime.

### D9. Minor internal inconsistencies

- **Gemini:** step 1 duration is "1 yr" in the text but 0.5–1 yr in the YAML. The YAML evidence list holds one unsure item.
- **Claude:** P1 is "literature + experiment" in the text but `method: literature` in the YAML.

Neither changes the ratings.

---

## 4. Evidence cited

No model cites any process evidence obtained in microgravity. The two-model, confident citations (Nakamura, Jarosewich) define the **feed**; they say nothing about separator performance. All process-relevant evidence is from 1 g or is physics-level only.

| Evidence | Cited by | Confidence as marked | What it supports | Flag |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Nakamura et al. 2011, *Science* (Itokawa = LL-chondrite material) | Claude, GPT | Both confident | Feed definition only | Best-attested item |
| Jarosewich 1990, *Meteoritics* (H/L/LL bulk metal) | Claude, GPT | Both confident. Claude is only medium on its own derived percentages. | Feed grade envelope | Best-attested item |
| Oder (& Taylor) 1990, lunar soil magnetic beneficiation | Claude, Gemini | **Both marked unsure** | 1 g, grams to kg | Only process-relevant item cited by two models; neither could verify it. Needs bibliographic verification. |
| Tsuchiyama et al. 2011, *Science* (Itokawa 3-D structure) | Claude only | Confident | Feed particle structure | Single-model |
| Murdoch et al. 2013, *PRL* 110, 018307 (granular flow in parabolic flight) | Claude only | Confident | Physics of the regime, not a separator | Single-model |
